- **PKG-FR-OPT-IN**: Every package job MUST ship disabled and MUST be enabled individually in configuration.
  Why: enabling one authorises the system to install and remove software on the target.
- **PKG-FR-JOB-INDEPENDENCE**: Each package sync job MUST be enableable, reviewable and failable on its own. Enabling one MUST NOT enable another, and no package sync job's behaviour may depend on whether another package sync job is enabled. What jobs outside package sync do with that information is not this article's business.
- **PKG-FR-JOB-ORDER**: All four package jobs — the three package managers and the job for software none of them can reproduce — MUST run before `folder_sync`, and the system MUST refuse to start when they are ordered otherwise.

- **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-SCOPE**: `flatpak_sync` MUST cover installed flatpak applications per flatpak installation scope, the remotes those applications need, and mask patterns per scope.
- **PKG-FR-MANUAL-SCOPE**: `manual_installs_sync` MUST cover what no package manager can reproduce — apt packages whose installed version comes from no repository the machine has configured, and software under `/usr/local` and `/opt` that no package owns — together with the registry of install snippets that is the only way such software can be reproduced on the other machine. The filesystem scan MUST cover `/opt`, every entry directly under `/usr/local`, and the entries of `/usr/local`'s `bin`, `sbin`, `lib`, `games` and `src`; it MUST NOT cover `/usr/local`'s `etc`, `include`, `man` or `share`. A finding may be a file, a directory or a symlink; it MUST be named at the path where it was found and MUST NOT be descended into. It is NOT a finding if a package owns it, if it is one of the entries `base-files` creates directly under `/usr/local`, or if it is a directory with no file anywhere beneath it.
  Why the four exclusions: what a hand install puts in `etc`, `include`, `man` or `share` arrives with an application the scan finds elsewhere, so scanning them adds a second finding for software already named once.
  Why a finding is not opened: one application under `/opt` or `/usr/local` is a whole tree, and walking it would ask the user about thousands of files that are one decision.
  Why the `base-files` entries: the distribution creates `/usr/local`'s own subdirectories and no package need own them, so presenting one would ask every user, on every machine, on every run, to write an install snippet for a stock directory whose contents the scan already names one level deeper. Every directory this scan descends into is one of them, so a scanned directory is never a finding of its own scan.
  Why the empty directory: a directory holding no file anywhere beneath it is a leftover shape rather than software, and there is nothing a snippet could reproduce.
- **PKG-FR-DEB-OWNERSHIP**: Software installed from a hand-downloaded `.deb` MUST belong to `manual_installs_sync` alone. `apt_sync` MUST NOT produce an item, a review line or an install for it in any configuration.

# Package Sync Specification

**Domain Code**: `PKG` (Package Management Sync, Phase 2)

## Navigation

- [System Documentation](_index.md)
- [Architecture](architecture.md)
- [Data Model](data-model.md) — item identity, the machine-local decision file and the install-snippet registry
- [Core Spec](core.md)
- [Package sync (user guide)](../jobs/package-sync.md)
- [Package sync — user requirements](../planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md) — the intent this spec implements
- [Package sync conformance criteria](../planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) — the checkable articles this spec is verified against

Four `SyncJob`s — `apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync` — replicate *what is installed* (apt packages plus the `/etc/apt` repository state they depend on, snaps, flatpaks, and the things no package manager can reproduce) rather than user data. The convergence model they implement is ADR-020: the source captures a manifest, the target diffs its own state against it, and each ecosystem's own tooling does the converging.

All four sit in the orchestrator's job-execution phase **ahead of `folder_sync`**: apps must exist before their data lands on top of them, `manual_installs_sync` included, since a replayed snippet installs software that writes its own defaults exactly as a package's postinst does. `Orchestrator._check_package_jobs_precede_folder_sync` validates the resolved, enabled order and refuses to start a run ordered otherwise.

## Shared core contract (`PackageSyncJob`)

`PackageSyncJob` is an abstract `SyncJob` every package-manager job subclasses. It declares two abstract hooks a concrete job implements:

- `plan()` — capture the source's manifest, query the target, diff the two, and build this job's review groups. Read-only. Each manager writes its own: what a diff even IS differs per ecosystem, so there is no base implementation to inherit — only the pieces every implementation uses (`filter_inert` on the way in, `_drop_inert_diffs` on the way out, `_build_review_groups` at the end).
- `converge(diff)` — apply one approved diff on the target. May raise `ConvergeItemFailed` to refuse an item without attempting its mutating command (e.g. a transaction-safety guard), or return a `CommandResult` whose non-zero exit code is treated as a per-item failure the same way. It may also raise `ConvergeItemDeclined` for an item the user withdrew after the review: neither applied nor failed, named in its own summary line, and never part of `PackageItemFailures`.

What the base class holds is what all four managers genuinely share: the plan/review/apply order, the machine-local decision-file rules, the review grouping and the converge loop. A manager's own item shapes, its own diff and the facts only it can collect live in that manager's module — a base class holding one manager's logic makes the other three inherit a surface they never use.

In return, the base class guarantees:

- **Planning is read-only.** `plan()` issues only read commands on both machines; nothing may mutate either machine until a review has been accepted.

Two agents are running in isolated worktrees: #248 (apt timers) and #219+#218 (JobResult SKIPPED + per-job summary). Both are forbidden from touching ADR-020 and from touching each other's files. #245 → #255 follow once #219 lands, since a flag-answered headless run and the SKIPPED rule are the same decision point.

Now the two you want to discuss.

## #246 — is tightening enough?

No, and your instinct is right for a concrete reason, not taste. I compared ADR-020 against the docs that already exist:

| Doc | Lines | Declared role |
|---|---|---|
| `planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md` | 322 | the intent |
| `planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md` | 394 | checkable `PKG-FR-*` articles; declares itself the authority over everything downstream |
| `system/package-sync.md` | 125 | how it's implemented |
| `jobs/package-sync.md` | 378 | operator's guide |
| `adr/adr-020` | 323 | "the decision record behind the model" |

ADR-020 lines 11–41 are an **"Implementation Rules"** block of ~30 dense MUST / MUST NOT clauses. That is a second normative rule set covering the same obligations as `PKG-FR-*`, with no stated precedence between them — and the conformance doc's own precedence chain doesn't mention it. It also cites zero `D-nn`, so the two rule sets aren't even cross-linked. That's a defect: two homes for one fact, and nothing says which wins.

The second mismatch is document *type*, not level. D-07 and D-24 carry screen-copy grammar — which words each answer key shows, that hostnames appear in every title and `source`/`target` never do, how a legend sentence is phrased. That's a UI specification living in an ADR.

So what's actually wrong is duplication and mixed types. The *structure* — one ADR holding D-01…D-43 — is good and worth keeping; 774 citations from `src/` and `tests/` depend on those IDs resolving, and they're a genuinely useful anchor.

My proposal, which is bigger than tightening but smaller than a split:

1. Delete the "Implementation Rules" block. First audit every clause in it for a `PKG-FR-*` counterpart; where one is missing, add the article to the conformance doc. Net effect: one normative home, and the precedence chain finally covers everything.
2. Move the screen-copy grammar out of D-07/D-24 into `system/package-sync.md`. D-07 keeps the decision — three-way by default, two answers for these cases, report-only takes none — and loses the paragraphs on wording.
3. Move measured evidence (the apt 2.8.3 filename rules, and the like) to `docs/adr/considerations/`, where the flatpak filter measurements already live.
4. Every `D-nn` ID and its section stays put. No citation breaks.

Result is roughly 150–180 lines: TL;DR, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives. The thing that bothers you goes away because the ADR stops being three documents.

On "should I get over it": partly. D-04 (versions float) and D-30 (collateral) genuinely aren't architecture — they're product rules. But recording them in the ADR is defensible, because they're *why* there's no version-pinning machinery. One sentence each, pointing at the user-requirements section that owns the intent, is the right size.

## #207 — scope and design

You didn't pick a convergence model, so here's the real fork rather than my preferred option restated.

First, a scope note: **#247 is the same issue as #207.** #207's body is #247 restructured with registry reconciliation folded in. #245 defers the registry case to "#247". I'd keep #207 as the design issue and label #247 `status: duplicate` — I won't close it.

What I verified about today's code:

- Exactly two origins exist: `apt-no-candidate` and `unowned-path`. `/opt` vs `/usr/local` is *not* an origin distinction — both are `unowned-path`; `/opt` only differs in that a "is this one application?" shape question runs.
- A registry entry is `{item_id, label, body, authored_at, authored_on}`. No version, no hash, no manifest of what the snippet produced — nothing to compare against.
- `plan()` subtracts every item the target holds *before* consulting the registry. Presence is the whole test.
- Reusable machinery exists: batched `sha256sum` digest capture already in the apt probe and `folder_sync`.

**The part I think is settled.** The `.deb` half is easy and should not be argued over: `dpkg-query` already knows the version on both machines, so a version diff is a one-command read, and an upgrade converges by replaying the snippet. One guarantee worth building in: after a replay, re-read the version — if it didn't move, fail the item naming the snippet as stale, rather than reporting success on a version-pinned snippet that will never upgrade anything.

That does need an explicit exception to D-04 ("versions float; a mismatch is reported, never forced"). D-04 holds because a repo will eventually move the package. For manual installs nothing will ever move it, so a version difference has to be actionable here or the job is back to reporting drift forever.

**The genuine fork is the path payloads.** Three options and none is clean:

- *Mirror the tree.* Deterministic, no idempotence assumption. But the extent is wrong: an `/opt` install typically also drops `/usr/share/applications/foo.desktop`, symlinks in `/usr/local/bin`, sometimes a systemd unit — and the scan covers only `/opt` and `/usr/local`. Mirroring the tree converges part of the software and silently leaves the rest.
- *Replay the snippet.* Extent is whatever the snippet does, which is correct by construction. But it assumes idempotence, which nothing today requires or asserts, and re-running an installer over a live tree can do anything.
- *Detect and report only.* Drift becomes visible — which is the actual bug, since today it's invisible forever — and the user resolves it. Smallest new surface, but leaves the job still converging nothing for that class.

I lean **replay, with drift detected by a cheap digest and the user answering per item**: one `find … -printf '%s %T@ %m %U %G %p'` per item path, digested, batched into a single command per host per sync. That catches an in-place upgrade without hashing 300 MB of `/opt/google/chrome` every run. Replay is already the convergence mechanism the job has, so the new thing being built is the *detection*, and idempotence becomes a documented requirement on snippets rather than an unstated assumption. But if you'd rather not put that requirement on snippets, "detect and report" is a defensible v1 and leaves the mechanism choice open.

**Removals** are more tractable than the issue implies. Both inverses are well-defined — `apt-get remove <name>` for a `.deb`, `rm -rf <path>` for a scanned path. The question is whether you want the job performing `rm -rf` on a root-owned tree off a review tick, or whether a registry entry should carry an authored `uninstall` body alongside its `install` body, symmetrical with how it got there. The second is safer and more work; the first is free but sharp. Either way the review line must say the removal is incomplete when the snippet put things outside the scanned path.

**Registry reconciliation** I'd fold in as you scoped it: merge per `item_id` using `authored_at`/`authored_on`, and raise a review item only when both machines edited the same entry. That deletes the whole-file abort, which is what blocks #245 from covering the case.

Four questions, then I'll write the ADR and the phase plan:

1. Path payloads — replay, mirror, or detect-and-report for v1?
2. Removal — derived default (`rm -rf` / `apt-get remove`), or an authored uninstall body in the registry?
3. Does D-04 get the explicit "manual installs are the exception, nothing floats here" carve-out?
4. #246 — proceed with the four-step proposal above? And do you want it run through Opus 4.8 as you suggested — I'd shell out to `claude -p --model <4.8 id>` since the subagent model picker only offers `sonnet`/`opus`/`haiku`/`fable`.

Implement GitHub issue #245 in /home/janfr/dev/pc-switcher (repo `pc-switcher`). Read the issue in full first: `gh issue view 245` — it contains a decision table and an explicit out-of-scope list that are the specification; follow them exactly. Read CLAUDE.md, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, docs/dev/development-guide.md and docs/dev/testing-guide.md before writing code.

You are in your own git worktree. Branch off `main`, commit as you go, push, and open a **draft** PR targeting `main` (draft is mandatory — it keeps integration tests from running prematurely). Reference `Fixes #245` in the PR body. Do not close the issue.

## What to build

Two CLI flags scoped to every `PackageSyncJob` subclass (`apt_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `snap_sync`, `manual_installs_sync`) and to nothing else:

- `--apply-package-installs` — apply every install-direction review item.
- `--apply-package-removals` — apply every removal-direction review item.

They answer as the source dictates, not as the screen's pre-selection suggests. Neither records a permanent (skip-always) machine-specific mark — `02-02-PLAN.md` forbids an unattended run writing one. `--yes` keeps its current meaning (the configuration-sync prompt, nothing else) and must still not answer a package review.

The issue's table maps review groups to flags; the "Out of scope" list enumerates groups no flag answers — those are skipped for this run and named in a warning, exactly as a no-TTY run does today. The non-additive registry transfer still **aborts** rather than skipping.

## Where things are (verified — check each before relying on it)

**Flag plumbing (Typer, five hops):** `cli.py:131` `main()` signature — existing `typer.Option`s at `--dry-run` :234, `--yes/-y` :241, `--confirm-each-command` :272 (:294 shows the pattern for a flag that refuses a non-TTY, which is the *inverse* of what you want here). Then `_run_sync(...)` call :308 / signature :322-329 → `_run_sync_async` :360-366 → `Orchestrator(...)` ~:407-411 → `Orchestrator.__init__` params :274-279 → and the ONLY way to reach a job: `_create_job_context()` → `JobContext(...)` `orchestrator.py:359-378`. **`JobContext` is `src/pcswitcher/jobs/context.py:18`** — add fields there. Note `--yes` (`auto_accept`) deliberately never reaches jobs (it is consumed at `orchestrator.py:763` → `config_sync.py`); keep it that way.

**Review path:** `src/pcswitcher/jobs/packages/review.py` — `Decision` StrEnum :320 (`APPLY`/`SKIP_ONCE`/`SKIP_ALWAYS`), `ReviewGroup` :293 (fields incl. the `overwrites_authored_content` flag), `ReviewOutcome` :335 (`decisions, was_interactive, snippets, unresolved`), `asks_for_a_decision(group)` :353, `_default_decision` :430, `_REMOVAL_ACTIONS` :177 (`remove/delete/disable/repo_removal`), `_PROMOTABLE_ACTIONS` :187, `_REPORT_ACTION` :195, `UNREPRODUCIBLE_REVIEW_ACTION` :207, `COLLATERAL_REVIEW_ACTION` :220, `REPO_CONFLICT_REVIEW_ACTION` :232, `REPO_REMOVAL_REVIEW_ACTION` ~:165. Entry point `review_items` ~:1130; the no-TTY branch that forces every entry to SKIP_ONCE is :1164-1174 with `_warn_every_item_unasked` :1122. `overwrites_authored_content` is set only at `sync_core.py:604` (apt config CHANGE).

**Existing precedent you must study before designing:** `PCSWITCHER_PACKAGE_REVIEW_AUTOMATION` (env var, `review.py:159`, consumed ~:1158 via `_decisions_from_automation` :688) already injects decisions non-interactively and returns `was_interactive=True`. Decide deliberately whether the new flags reuse that seam, sit beside it, or replace it, and justify the choice in the PR body.

## Three subtleties that will bite you — handle each explicitly and say what you did

1. **`was_interactive` is overloaded.** `sync_core.py:882` (`_record_permanent_skips`) guards on `_accepted_outcome_was_interactive()` so nothing is recorded permanently on a non-interactive run — the flags MUST NOT write marks, so that guard must keep holding. But `sync_core.py:1004` raises `JobSkipped` when any group `asks_for_a_decision` and the outcome was not interactive — a flag-answered run that actually converges must NOT be reported as skipped. And a run where the flags answer *nothing* (every group out of scope) must still skip. One boolean cannot express all three; introduce whatever distinguishes "answered by policy" from "nobody answered", and keep the mark-recording guard keyed to human interaction.

2. **`after_review()` only runs when the outcome was interactive** (`sync_core.py` execute, ~:1004-1011). For `manual_installs_sync` that hook is what pushes the snippet registry to the target (`manual_installs_sync.py:287` → `_push_snippet_registry` :345) — and `converge()` :1000 replays from the **target's** registry. So if `--apply-package-installs` approves a manual install whose snippet exists on the source, the registry push must still happen or the replay reads a stale or absent registry. Work out what must run and what must not (snippet *authoring* needs a TTY and stays out of scope), and cover it with a test.

3. **Collateral coupling** (already noted in the issue): skipping a collateral entry also leaves the changes that cause it unapproved (`AptSyncJob.accept_review`, `apt_sync/job.py:880`), so `--apply-package-installs` alone will not converge an install whose transaction removes a protected package. Verify this actually behaves as the issue states and document the observed behaviour in the PR — do not just repeat the claim.

## Docs and coverage (all required)

- `docs/dev/package-sync-scenario-coverage.md` — a row per new behaviour, same as the behaviours these flags override. Header `| # | Scenario | Expected | Cov | Test |`; IDs are stable, never renumbered, appended at the end of their section; tests cite IDs in the FIRST clause of the docstring, comma-separated then `—`. `tests/unit/test_scenario_coverage_matrix.py` enforces the two-way link both ways. Scenario H162 (`--yes` must not answer a package review) and G70-G75 (registry-overwrite abort under `--yes`) must still hold — extend, don't replace.
- `docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md` — new `PKG-FR-*` articles for what the flags guarantee and what they refuse to answer. Follow the house style: id, MUST/MUST NOT clause, then a `Why:` line.
- `docs/jobs/package-sync.md` "Non-interactive runs" (~:267) and `docs/system/package-sync.md`; plus README/CLI help if flags are listed there.

## Hard constraints

- **Do NOT edit `docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md`** — it is being restructured separately. Put any needed ADR wording in the PR body under "ADR follow-up needed".
- Two other branches are in flight. **PR #259** (`fix/job-skipped-and-summary`) removed the CLI's end-of-run failure list and added a per-job outcome summary in `orchestrator.py`, and touched the `JobResult` construction sites. Stay out of `cli.py`'s end-of-run output region and out of `orchestrator.py`'s `JobResult`/summary code; your orchestrator edit is the `JobContext` construction at :359-378 and the `__init__` params only. A separate branch owns `orchestrator.py`'s snapd/apt-timer hold region (:78-101, :327-338, :1438-1683) and all of `src/pcswitcher/jobs/apt_sync/**` **except** `job.py:880` `accept_review` if you genuinely need it — if you do, keep the edit surgical and say so.
- Do not add the review follow-up screen for machine-specific mark placement — that is #255, a separate branch that will also edit `review.py`. Keep your `review.py` changes confined to the answering/defaulting path.
- Every executor call that reaches a machine needs `mutates=` unless purely read-only; `tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py` enforces it.
- Stage explicit paths; never `git add -A`. Never `git stash`.

## Definition of done

`uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format . && uv run codespell && uv run basedpyright && uv run pytest` all clean. Draft PR open. Then run `~/.claude/skills/wait-for-ci/wait-github-ci.sh <pr>` as a background bash task and report the final CI result.

Return: PR number + URL, branch name, how you resolved the `was_interactive` overload, what you found about `after_review`/registry push and about the collateral coupling (verified, not inferred), and anything left out. Be terse.

168:+        was never cleaned up is left with nothing of this run's beyond the restored timers.
169:+        """

174:+            f"--unit={_APT_TIMER_RESTORE_UNIT} --description={shlex.quote(description)} {start}"
175:+        )

input.summary: Fix reboot claim in apt timer comment
input.message:
CI is green on #260 (Lint, Unit Tests, CI Status pass; Integration skipped as expected for a draft). I reviewed the orchestrator diff. The design is right — schedule-before-stop, per-host capture gating, restore-then-cancel ordering, `_running_apt_timers` restricting the restore to exactly what was taken. Two comment corrections, then you're done.

1. **The reboot claim is false.** `src/pcswitcher/orchestrator.py`, the `_APT_TIMER_SUSPENSION` comment block (~line 29-31 of the added region) says the transient unit "survives the sync being killed, the SSH connection dropping and the machine rebooting into a run that never reached `_cleanup`". A `systemd-run` transient unit lives in `/run/systemd/transient/`, which is tmpfs — it does not survive a reboot. The safety property still holds across a reboot, but by a different mechanism: `systemctl stop` is runtime state too, so an enabled timer starts again at boot on its own. Verify both halves of that yourself (`systemd-run` transience and stop non-persistence) rather than taking my word, then rewrite the comment to claim only what the mechanism actually does and name the boot path as the separate reason a reboot is covered.

2. **`_APT_TIMER_RESTORE_UNIT`'s "needs no special handling" is overstated.** The reasoning holds only while nobody touches the machine. If a run dies and the user then starts the timers by hand, the next run reads them active, tries `systemd-run --unit=pc-switcher-apt-timers`, and the name is still taken — so that host is warned about and left unsuspended. That is the right failure direction, but it is a case the comment currently says cannot happen. Reword to state the fail-safe rather than claim the case away.

Comments only — no behaviour change, no new tests. Keep both terse. Then re-run `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format . && uv run codespell && uv run basedpyright && uv run pytest`, commit, push, and confirm CI. Report back only: commit sha, and what you found when you verified the two systemd claims.

# Task: GitHub issue #246 — clean up ADR-020

Repo: `/home/janfr/dev/pc-switcher`. You are already in an isolated git worktree at `.claude/worktrees/adr-020-cleanup`, on branch `docs/adr-020-cleanup`, based on `origin/main`. Work only there.

Read first: `CLAUDE.md`, `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `docs/adr/adr-001-adr.md` (ADR instructions), `gh issue view 246`.

**Terseness is the deliverable, not a side constraint.** The file is 323 lines of prose that says things three times. Cut hard. Every sentence that does not change what a reader concludes goes.

## The problem

ADR-020 is three documents in one:

1. A decision record (`## Decision`, sections `D-01`..`D-43`) — this is what an ADR is for, and it stays.
2. An `## Implementation Rules` block (lines 11-41) of MUST / Forbidden clauses — a second normative rule set covering the same obligations as `docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md`'s `PKG-FR-*` / `PKG-NG-*` articles, with no declared precedence between the two. That doc declares itself authoritative over everything downstream and never cites a `D-nn`; the two rule sets are not even cross-linked.
3. Screen-copy rules (which words each answer key shows, that hostnames appear in every title and `source`/`target` never do, how a legend sentence reads) embedded in `D-07` and `D-24` — a UI specification.

Plus measured third-party-tool evidence ("measured against apt 2.8.3", filename rules) inline in the decision prose.

## What to do

1. **Delete the `## Implementation Rules` block.** Before deleting, audit every clause in it for a `PKG-FR-*` / `PKG-NG-*` counterpart. Where a clause has no counterpart anywhere, add the article to `docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md` in that doc's house style (id, MUST/MUST NOT clause, then a `Why:` line) so no obligation is lost. Net effect: one normative home, and the precedence chain finally covers everything.
2. **Move the screen-copy grammar out of `D-07` and `D-24`** into `docs/system/package-sync.md`. Each decision keeps the decision — `D-07`: three-way by default, two answers for the enumerated cases, report-only takes no answer; `D-24`: reviews are batched per manager per action, and when a job may ask again — and loses the paragraphs on wording.
3. **Move measured evidence to `docs/adr/considerations/`.** A file `docs/adr/considerations/adr-020-*.md` already exists for the flatpak filter measurements; put the rest alongside it, following that file's shape. Link from the ADR.
4. **Trim the surviving prose.** Target roughly 150-180 lines total: TL;DR, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered, References.

`D-04` (versions float) and `D-30` (collateral) are product rules rather than architecture. Keep them — they are why there is no version-pinning machinery — but at one or two sentences each, pointing at the section of `docs/planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md` that owns the intent.

## Non-negotiable constraints

- **Every `D-nn` id and its section heading stays in ADR-020.** `src/` and `tests/` carry 774 citations of the form `D-07`, `D-30` and so on; each must still resolve to a section in this file. You may shorten a section's prose to a sentence. You may not delete, renumber, merge or rehome one.
- **Docs only.** Do not touch anything under `src/` or `tests/`, except that if a code comment cites a `D-nn` whose meaning you changed, stop and report it instead of editing.
- **No history, no archaeology.** Do not write "previously this said", "moved from", "formerly", changelog notes or dated incidents. Fix the artifact and stop. This applies to the ADR, the commits and the PR body.
- Markdown house rules: one paragraph = one line, no hard-wrapping mid-sentence; `---` only as frontmatter, never a separator; real heading levels, never bold as a pseudo-heading.
- Where a fact ends up in two files, one of them is wrong. Decide the home and link from the other.

## Collision warning

Three other branches are in flight and two of them also edit `docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md`, appending new `PKG-FR-*` articles at the ends of sections. Expect a merge conflict there and keep your additions appended at section ends so it resolves cleanly. Do **not** touch `docs/dev/package-sync-scenario-coverage.md` at all — three branches are appending rows to it, and this change needs none.

## Definition of done

`uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format . && uv run codespell && uv run basedpyright && uv run pytest` clean (docs-only, but some tests assert doc content — `tests/unit/test_scenario_coverage_matrix.py` among them). Report back, terse: PR number and URL, the ADR's line count before and after, how many clauses were DUPLICATE vs ORPHAN in the audit, which orphans became new `PKG-FR-*` articles, and anything you deliberately left in place.

1. A decision record (`## Decision`, sections `D-01`..`D-43`) — this is what an ADR is for, and it stays.

1. **Delete the `## Implementation Rules` block.** Before deleting, audit every clause in it for a `PKG-FR-*` / `PKG-NG-*` counterpart. What I found verifying the two systemd claims — you were right on both:

1. **Reboot claim was false.** `man systemd.unit`'s system unit search path lists `/run/systemd/transient/*`, described in the load-path table as "Dynamic configuration for transient units", and `findmnt /run` reports `tmpfs` — so a `systemd-run` unit is gone at the next boot. The safety property does still hold across a reboot, by the mechanism you named: `systemctl stop` writes nothing to disk (only `enable`/`disable`/`mask` touch the unit-file tree, and only those honour `--runtime` for "until the next reboot"), so an enabled timer is pulled back in at boot by its `[Install]` section — confirmed on `apt-daily.timer`: `WantedBy=timers.target`, `UnitFileState=enabled`. The comment now claims only killed-process and dropped-connection coverage for the transient unit, and names the boot path as the separate, disjoint reason a reboot is covered.

2. **The stale-unit case is reachable**, exactly as you described: a died run plus a user starting the timers by hand gets past the inactive-timers skip and hits the taken name. The comment now states the fail-safe — `_apply_apt_timer_suspension` warns and leaves that host unsuspended while the predecessor's pending unit still covers the machine — and says why clearing the name first would be worse (it destroys that cover for the width of the reschedule).

No behaviour change, no new tests; `ruff`, `codespell`, `basedpyright` and 4730 tests clean locally before pushing.

## #207 — challenging the spec

Order noted: #253 → #251 → #252, then design #207 across all four jobs. #247 folded in, won't mention it again.

Seven things, roughly by how much they'd hurt.

**1. Don't replay before you know something differs.** "If snippet body changed, always apply snippet first" mutates ahead of the evidence. A body edit is often cosmetic — a comment, a mirror URL, a version bump in a `wget` line that resolves to what's already installed — and the installed result on both machines can be identical. Replaying an installer over a working install to discover it changed nothing is the highest-blast-radius operation in the design, spent for no information. Detect body drift *and* result drift in the same plan pass, then show one screen per item naming both facts, then act. Your objection is presumably that you can't know whether the new snippet fixes the payload difference until you run it — true, but you can know whether a difference exists, and that's what the user is deciding on. This also asks fewer rounds, which your own batching preference wants.

**2. "Apply new snippet" has no referent in the case you scoped it to.** Both branches are gated on "snippet didn't change" — so there is no new snippet to apply and the three answers collapse to two. I think you mean *author a fresh snippet now and apply that*, reusing the on-the-fly authoring path the job already has for unreproducible items. If so the spec is fine and just needs saying. If you meant something else, this is the pivot of the whole design and I'd rather not guess.

**3. The loop doesn't terminate.** "Apply, re-check, if still different get back to user, loop." A version-pinned snippet — fixed URL, fixed tarball — will never move the version, so replaying it a second time cannot help and the loop asks forever. Rule: at most one replay per item per run; if it doesn't converge, stop and report, naming the snippet as the thing that needs editing. Without that, a headless run spins.

**4. Purge — my answer is no by default, and don't ask up front.** Three reasons. Purging destroys what the *user* put in the tree: licences, plugins, profiles, config under `/opt/foo`. Most installers overwrite in place anyway, so the purge buys nothing in the common case. And a purge-then-replay that fails halfway leaves the machine with *nothing* where a working install used to be — strictly worse than the drift being fixed. Instead make it the second answer, offered only once a plain replay has demonstrably failed to converge: "replace — remove the path, then run the snippet". That ties the destructive option to evidence rather than a guess, and it gives point 3 its terminating step.

**5. Version direction is unhandled.** "Version A != version B" doesn't say who is newer. If the target is newer, replaying the source's snippet is a downgrade or a no-op — a different act from the target-older case, and one the user would answer differently. The screen must name both machines and both versions, and say which way it goes. Decide whether target-newer is offered for apply at all, or is report-only.

**6. Removal needs a mechanism, not just an item.** The item is the easy half. Applying it isn't uniform: `apt-get remove`, `snap remove`, `flatpak uninstall` are clean; `rm -rf <path>` is sharp *and* incomplete, because a snippet that installed into `/opt/foo` typically also dropped a `.desktop` file, a symlink in `/usr/local/bin`, sometimes a systemd unit — all outside the scanned path, none of them removed. Either a registry entry gains an authored uninstall body, symmetrical with how it got installed, or the screen states plainly that the removal covers only that path. Pick one; silently leaving debris is the option to avoid.

**7. The genuinely unsolved bit: what "contents changed" means for a path.** A full-tree digest will report drift forever on any application that writes inside its own directory — logs, caches, plugin state, machine-local config. That class becomes a permanent false-positive generator and users learn to ignore it, which costs you the real detections too. Options: record a manifest of what the snippet produced at replay time and compare only those files (works for anything pc-switcher installed, gives nothing for pre-existing items); or let a registry entry carry ignore globs; or both, with the manifest as the default and globs as the escape hatch. I don't think the path class is worth building until this is decided.

One smaller note: a "which snippet" answer is neither an install nor a removal, so #245's `--apply-package-installs`/`--apply-package-removals` can't answer it — it behaves like an `unreproducible` item, which #245 puts out of scope. Headless runs should skip drift items with a warning, and the ADR should say so, or the two features will read as contradicting each other.

#245 landed: PR #261, CI green. Two findings from it worth keeping: the collateral coupling in the issue was **measured, not assumed** — with `--apply-package-installs` alone no `apt-get install` is issued at all, because the collateral group belongs to the removal flag and its `SKIP_ONCE` propagates onto the triggering install. Implement GitHub issue #255 in /home/janfr/dev/pc-switcher (repo `pc-switcher`). Read `gh issue view 255` first. Read CLAUDE.md, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, docs/dev/development-guide.md, docs/dev/testing-guide.md, and `docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md` (sections D-07, D-08/D-08a, D-24) before writing code.

You are in your own git worktree. Branch off `main`, commit as you go, push, and open a **draft** PR targeting `main` (draft is mandatory). Reference `Fixes #255` in the PR body. Do not close the issue.

## What to build

When "always skip" (`Decision.SKIP_ALWAYS`) is answered on a **conflicting** item — one both machines hold with different content, `DiffAction.CHANGE` — the machine-specific mark is currently always written on the target. Let the user choose which side it lands on: source, target, or both.

**The UX is decided — implement this shape.** The batch review screen keeps its three answers unchanged. content.content:
1	# ADR-020: Declarative package convergence — a package replicates as (name, origin), and repository configuration follows the packages approved from it
2	
3	Status: Draft
4	
5	Date: 2026-07-23
6	
7	## TL;DR
8	
9	The source captures a manifest of package-related items; the target diffs its own state against it and converges using `apt`, `snap` and `flatpak` themselves — package databases are never rsynced. A package replicates as (name, origin), not name: the review decides packages and apt config, while repositories, their keys, pins, flatpak remotes and blocks — apt holds, snap refresh holds, flatpak masks — are all derived, replicated because the software they serve is and never reviewed at all. Four independent jobs (`apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync`) each run plan then review then apply inside their own `execute()`, every change approved before it is made and the questions batched into one screen per manager per action where the logic permits.
10	
11	## Context
12	
13	Phase 2 must replicate presence, version and provenance of packages across apt, snap and flatpak, plus the repository/keyring/pin/remote configuration those installs depend on. Package data under `~/.var/app`, `~/snap/<app>/common` and dotfiles is Phase 1 `folder_sync` territory; this ADR concerns the packages and the configuration that governs where they come from.
14	
15	Provenance is the hard part, because a package name is offered by more than one vendor: `firefox` exists in Ubuntu's archive and in Mozilla's own repository, and `org.mozilla.firefox` on Flathub and Flathub-beta. Matching by name alone replicates the name and inverts the provenance, silently and at exit 0. Replication is therefore of (name, origin), and the configuration that makes an origin reachable is mechanism serving that guarantee rather than something the user is asked about — a repository ticked without its package does nothing, a package ticked without its repository cannot be installed, and the pairing was never expressible in a checkbox list.
16	
17	The review boundary is the manager: each package job captures its own diff and surfaces it for decision before it applies anything, and no review spans more than a single manager's items — which keeps four deliberately independent jobs independent rather than binding them to a shared review with a common ordering and failure surface. The normative obligations these decisions imply are stated as checkable articles in [package-sync-conformance-criteria.md](../planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) (`PKG-FR-*`, `PKG-NG-*`); this ADR records the decisions, not a second rule set.
18	
19	## Decision
20	
21	### Convergence model (D-01)
22	
23	The source captures a manifest; the target diffs its own state against it and converges using `apt`, `snap` and `flatpak` themselves. `/var/lib/dpkg`, `/var/lib/snapd` and the flatpak OSTree store are never rsynced — the package managers stay authoritative for their own state.
24	
25	### Item model (D-02)
26	
27	An item is something the user can meaningfully decide about, carrying a stable identity through one diff → decide → apply pipeline. The item classes are the apt package, the apt config file, the snap, the snap channel, the flatpak ref, the unreproducible/manual install, and — for removal only — the apt source file and the apt pin file. A flatpak remote is not an item (D-41), and neither is a block — an apt hold, a snap refresh hold or a flatpak mask.
28	
29	A block keeps an identity of its own so the converge order (install before hold, masks after refs) and failure reporting can name it, but it is **derived**, not decided: it replicates because the software it applies to does, exactly as a pin does. Replicating every one costs nothing and cannot get a per-item derivation wrong, while asking about one separately let the user contradict the answer they gave about the software itself. A block that freezes an installed copy — an apt hold, a snap refresh hold — is not registered for software the target does not end the run with; a flatpak mask is a rule about what may be installed and still lands. An apt hold naming a package its own machine does not have freezes nothing while refusing every later install of that name: the run ends, naming the package and the machine. Mechanism the user has no basis to judge — repository files, signing keys, pins, flatpak remotes, and a transient guard a run sets and clears — is not an item and is the job's own business to keep correct (D-34, D-36, D-37, D-41).
30	
31	### Manifest content for apt (D-03)
32	
33	The manifest carries the manually-installed set from `apt-mark showmanual`, not the full dpkg selection set; apt resolves dependencies on the target.
34	
35	### Version policy (D-04, D-05)
36	
37	Versions float to whatever the target's repos currently offer, and a version mismatch is a reported diff class rather than a forced change — which is why there is no version-pinning machinery. The one exception inside apt is a held package, which takes the source's exact version, because an apt hold blocks install, upgrade and removal alike and so carries "do not move this off the version that works". This is a product rule; its intent is owned by [package-sync-user-requirements.md](../planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md#the-model). Deliberate `preferences.d` pins still travel (D-36) even though versions float.
38	
39	### Revision/scope convergence (D-06)
40	
41	The snap manifest carries name + channel + revision; the flatpak manifest carries ref + origin + user/system scope. Snap converges revision and channel, because snap is the only ecosystem that embeds the version in its per-user data path (`~/snap/<app>/<rev>`), so both machines on the same revision is what lets `folder_sync` mirror that data cleanly. snapd auto-refreshes in the background and could move a snap off the converged revision mid-run, so the orchestrator pauses snapd's automatic refresh across the sync window on both hosts, restoring each host's prior setting on cleanup and relying on a timeout so a crashed run leaves no pause behind. This gates only auto-refresh, not the explicit convergence, and never leaves a standing block on any manager's auto-update once a run ends.
42	
43	### Decision shape and direction (D-07)
44	
45	The default is a three-way decision: apply / skip once / skip always. A `REPORT_ONLY` item takes NO answer at all — it converges in neither direction and records nothing, so both answers would leave both machines identical; such items are printed, grouped by the `DiffClass` that caused them, each group carrying the remedy where there is one. "Apply" is direction-dependent: missing on target means install/add/enable, extra means remove/delete/disable, different on both means change the target to match the source. Two cases take **two** answers — act, or skip once — and record nothing: an apt source or pin removal (D-37), and the repository/remote-conflict overwrite prompts (D-37, D-41); a flatpak remote is never asked about (D-41). The grammar these screens and answers follow — hostnames not source/target, one answer per key, the answers read as a set — is specified in [package-sync.md](../system/package-sync.md) and its articles.
46	
47	### Machine-local decision file (D-08, D-08a, D-09, D-10, D-43)
48	
49	One file per manager lives at `~/.config/pc-switcher/<manager>.decisions.yaml`, never synced, excluded from `folder_sync` non-overridably and outside `config_sync`. An entry on machine M makes the item inert on M in both roles — not pushed when M is the source, not installed or removed when M is the target. It is written on the machine whose copy the answer keeps: an install declined for good on the source, a declined removal or overwrite on the target. An overwrite is the one direction whose holder the run's own direction cannot name — both machines have the item and the recorder takes the other role next sync — so an item both machines have is read back from both files and filtered out of both inventories (D-08a). An entry lasts as long as its item is on the machine holding it, and is dropped once that machine no longer has it (D-43), including when this run's own approved work took it (the collateral case D-30 allows). A dead entry is not the cautious option: it acts in both roles, so one naming absent software goes on refusing to install it there for good. The check is a positive statement that the machine lacks the item, never absence from the narrower inventory the diff was built from; a check that cannot answer drops nothing. Software that returns is a new item, reviewed again.
50	
51	### Repository configuration is derived mechanism (D-11, D-12, D-13, D-14)
52	
53	`/etc/apt` is not file-mirrored: a `--delete` mirror would wipe the target's own machine-specific sources, and it is not an inventory of reviewed items. Four buckets cover every file: derived from approved packages (repository files, their keyrings, conflict-free overwrites of a repository on both machines — D-34, D-37); always synced (every `preferences.d` pin — D-36 — and the distribution's own source files — D-38); reviewed with two answers (repository and pin removals, the repository-conflict overwrite — D-07, D-37); and reviewed with the full three-way decision (`apt.conf.d` — D-37). Only files apt itself reads are captured, compared or written, by each fragment directory's own extension and filename rule (D-13; the `.save`, `.distUpgrade`, `.dpkg-dist` and editor backups those directories collect are left alone, since treating one as configuration would propose a change apt would never act on — [measurements](considerations/adr-020-apt-esm-and-snap-measurements.md)). A repository's signing key travels with it byte-for-byte from the source, never re-fetched from a vendor (a fresh fetch would silently substitute whatever the vendor serves today); the same governs a flatpak remote's ostree keyring (D-41). A repository whose key cannot be made to work is reported, not written. Every repository, key, pin and remote an approved item needs is provisioned before the install that needs it (D-14): for apt the `/etc/apt` group converges ahead of the first `apt-get install`, for flatpak the derived remote writes run ahead of the first `flatpak install`.
54	
55	### Job split into four jobs (D-15, D-16, D-17, D-18)
56	
57	Four jobs — `apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync` — are four separate `SyncJob`s, never merged into one `package_sync`, over one shared core extracted while building. The core holds what all four use: the item taxonomy, the plan/review/apply order, the decision flow, the batched TUI review, the machine-local file I/O and the read-failure guard (ADR-022). Each manager's own item shapes and diff stay in that manager's module — one manager's diff on the shared base would make the other three inherit inputs they never supply. All four run before `folder_sync` so software is provisioned before its data lands (decisive for flatpak, where `~/.local/share/flatpak` must exist before `~/.var/app` arrives); a snippet-installed program writes its own stock defaults as a package does. `manual_installs_sync` owns everything no package manager can reproduce and carries its own enable flag.
58	
59	### Batched review inside each job (D-24)
60	
61	Each package job runs plan then review then apply inside its own `execute()` and converges only what the review approved. Batching — one screen per manager per action — is a strong preference, applied where the logic permits and abandoned where it does not: a job never turns a batch into a question per item, and never complicates or omits its logic to avoid another round. A job may ask again, including after it has begun writing, when the answer it needs rests on facts this run's own changes invalidated or that no read could establish before the first write; correctness outranks batching, always. `apt_sync` asks in rounds, and only `apt_sync`. Three of its questions are scoped to the work this run APPROVES rather than proposes — a repository not raised for deletion while an approved-surviving package still uses it, a repository conflict raised only for a file an approved package makes travel, and a package marked as the target's own — none decidable while the plan is built and all decidable once the first round's answers exist: a second round, same sitting, nothing written yet. The one thing unknowable before writing is the collateral of an install whose repository this run itself writes (D-40): a third round, asked once, before the first of those installs. The other three jobs have one round. No review spans two managers (D-15), so there is no shared review phase and no coordinator.
62	
63	### Diff taxonomy (D-25)
64	
65	Conflicts, mismatches and unavailability are diff classes inside the job's own review: missing-on-target, extra-on-target, version-mismatch (both versions shown), origin-mismatch, origin-unavailable, unreproducible. `ORIGIN_MISMATCH` covers a package or ref installed on both machines from different vendors. `REPO_UNAVAILABLE` means the source's origin cannot be provided on the target — a statement about provenance, not about whether apt printed a candidate. There is no per-package echo of a pin or a hold: D-35 checks a pin against the target's real state, and echoing it onto every package it names would make a pinned target-only package impossible to remove.
66	
67	### Transactional repository convergence (D-27 boundary)
68	
69	The `/etc/apt` group is the one place D-27's continue-and-report model does not apply: it is transactional, and a group whose metadata refresh fails leaves `/etc/apt` as it found it. Continuing past a bad write would leave the target's package manager unusable, and automatic snapshot rollback does not arrive until Phase 7.

# ADR-020: Declarative package convergence — a package replicates as (name, origin), and repository configuration follows the packages approved from it

Status: Draft

Date: 2026-07-23

## TL;DR

The source captures a manifest of package-related items; the target diffs its own state against it and converges using `apt`, `snap` and `flatpak` themselves — package databases are never rsynced. A package replicates as (name, origin), not name: the review decides packages and apt config, while repositories, their keys, pins, flatpak remotes and blocks — apt holds, snap refresh holds, flatpak masks — are all derived, replicated because the software they serve is and never reviewed at all. Four independent jobs (`apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync`) each run plan then review then apply inside their own `execute()`, every change approved before it is made and the questions batched into one screen per manager per action where the logic permits.

## Context

Phase 2 must replicate presence, version and provenance of packages across apt, snap and flatpak, plus the repository/keyring/pin/remote configuration those installs depend on. Package data under `~/.var/app`, `~/snap/<app>/common` and dotfiles is Phase 1 `folder_sync` territory; this ADR concerns the packages and the configuration that governs where they come from.

Provenance is the hard part, because a package name is offered by more than one vendor: `firefox` exists in Ubuntu's archive and in Mozilla's own repository, and `org.mozilla.firefox` on Flathub and Flathub-beta. Matching by name alone replicates the name and inverts the provenance, silently and at exit 0. Replication is therefore of (name, origin), and the configuration that makes an origin reachable is mechanism serving that guarantee rather than something the user is asked about — a repository ticked without its package does nothing, a package ticked without its repository cannot be installed, and the pairing was never expressible in a checkbox list.

The review boundary is the manager: each package job captures its own diff and surfaces it for decision before it applies anything, and no review spans more than a single manager's items — which keeps four deliberately independent jobs independent rather than binding them to a shared review with a common ordering and failure surface. The normative obligations these decisions imply are stated as checkable articles in [package-sync-conformance-criteria.md](../planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) (`PKG-FR-*`, `PKG-NG-*`); this ADR records the decisions, not a second rule set.

## Decision

### Convergence model (D-01)

The source captures a manifest; the target diffs its own state against it and converges using `apt`, `snap` and `flatpak` themselves. `/var/lib/dpkg`, `/var/lib/snapd` and the flatpak OSTree store are never rsynced — the package managers stay authoritative for their own state.

### Item model (D-02)

An item is something the user can meaningfully decide about, carrying a stable identity through one diff → decide → apply pipeline. The item classes are the apt package, the apt config file, the snap, the snap channel, the flatpak ref, the unreproducible/manual install, and — for removal only — the apt source file and the apt pin file. A flatpak remote is not an item (D-41), and neither is a block — an apt hold, a snap refresh hold or a flatpak mask.

A block keeps an identity of its own so the converge order (install before hold, masks after refs) and failure reporting can name it, but it is **derived**, not decided: it replicates because the software it applies to does, exactly as a pin does. Replicating every one costs nothing and cannot get a per-item derivation wrong, while asking about one separately let the user contradict the answer they gave about the software itself. A block that freezes an installed copy — an apt hold, a snap refresh hold — is not registered for software the target does not end the run with; a flatpak mask is a rule about what may be installed and still lands. An apt hold naming a package its own machine does not have freezes nothing while refusing every later install of that name: the run ends, naming the package and the machine. Mechanism the user has no basis to judge — repository files, signing keys, pins, flatpak remotes, and a transient guard a run sets and clears — is not an item and is the job's own business to keep correct (D-34, D-36, D-37, D-41).

### Manifest content for apt (D-03)

The manifest carries the manually-installed set from `apt-mark showmanual`, not the full dpkg selection set; apt resolves dependencies on the target.

### Version policy (D-04, D-05)

Versions float to whatever the target's repos currently offer, and a version mismatch is a reported diff class rather than a forced change — which is why there is no version-pinning machinery. The one exception inside apt is a held package, which takes the source's exact version, because an apt hold blocks install, upgrade and removal alike and so carries "do not move this off the version that works". This is a product rule; its intent is owned by [package-sync-user-requirements.md](../planning/package-sync-user-requirements.md#the-model). Deliberate `preferences.d` pins still travel (D-36) even though versions float.

### Revision/scope convergence (D-06)

The snap manifest carries name + channel + revision; the flatpak manifest carries ref + origin + user/system scope. Snap converges revision and channel, because snap is the only ecosystem that embeds the version in its per-user data path (`~/snap/<app>/<rev>`), so both machines on the same revision is what lets `folder_sync` mirror that data cleanly. snapd auto-refreshes in the background and could move a snap off the converged revision mid-run, so the orchestrator pauses snapd's automatic refresh across the sync window on both hosts, restoring each host's prior setting on cleanup and relying on a timeout so a crashed run leaves no pause behind. This gates only auto-refresh, not the explicit convergence, and never leaves a standing block on any manager's auto-update once a run ends.

### Decision shape and direction (D-07)

The default is a three-way decision: apply / skip once / skip always. A `REPORT_ONLY` item takes NO answer at all — it converges in neither direction and records nothing, so both answers would leave both machines identical; such items are printed, grouped by the `DiffClass` that caused them, each group carrying the remedy where there is one. "Apply" is direction-dependent: missing on target means install/add/enable, extra means remove/delete/disable, different on both means change the target to match the source. Two cases take **two** answers — act, or skip once — and record nothing: an apt source or pin removal (D-37), and the repository/remote-conflict overwrite prompts (D-37, D-41); a flatpak remote is never asked about (D-41). The grammar these screens and answers follow — hostnames not source/target, one answer per key, the answers read as a set — is specified in [package-sync.md](../system/package-sync.md) and its articles.

### Machine-local decision file (D-08, D-08a, D-09, D-10, D-43)

One file per manager lives at `~/.config/pc-switcher/<manager>.decisions.yaml`, never synced, excluded from `folder_sync` non-overridably and outside `config_sync`. An entry on machine M makes the item inert on M in both roles — not pushed when M is the source, not installed or removed when M is the target. It is written on the machine whose copy the answer keeps: an install declined for good on the source, a declined removal or overwrite on the target. An overwrite is the one direction whose holder the run's own direction cannot name — both machines have the item and the recorder takes the other role next sync — so an item both machines have is read back from both files and filtered out of both inventories (D-08a). An entry lasts as long as its item is on the machine holding it, and is dropped once that machine no longer has it (D-43), including when this run's own approved work took it (the collateral case D-30 allows). A dead entry is not the cautious option: it acts in both roles, so one naming absent software goes on refusing to install it there for good. The check is a positive statement that the machine lacks the item, never absence from the narrower inventory the diff was built from; a check that cannot answer drops nothing. Software that returns is a new item, reviewed again.

### Repository configuration is derived mechanism (D-11, D-12, D-13, D-14)

`/etc/apt` is not file-mirrored: a `--delete` mirror would wipe the target's own machine-specific sources, and it is not an inventory of reviewed items. Four buckets cover every file: derived from approved packages (repository files, their keyrings, conflict-free overwrites of a repository on both machines — D-34, D-37); always synced (every `preferences.d` pin — D-36 — and the distribution's own source files — D-38); reviewed with two answers (repository and pin removals, the repository-conflict overwrite — D-07, D-37); and reviewed with the full three-way decision (`apt.conf.d` — D-37). Only files apt itself reads are captured, compared or written, by each fragment directory's own extension and filename rule (D-13; the `.save`, `.distUpgrade`, `.dpkg-dist` and editor backups those directories collect are left alone, since treating one as configuration would propose a change apt would never act on — [measurements](considerations/adr-020-apt-esm-and-snap-measurements.md)). A repository's signing key travels with it byte-for-byte from the source, never re-fetched from a vendor (a fresh fetch would silently substitute whatever the vendor serves today); the same governs a flatpak remote's ostree keyring (D-41). A repository whose key cannot be made to work is reported, not written. Every repository, key, pin and remote an approved item needs is provisioned before the install that needs it (D-14): for apt the `/etc/apt` group converges ahead of the first `apt-get install`, for flatpak the derived remote writes run ahead of the first `flatpak install`.

### Job split into four jobs (D-15, D-16, D-17, D-18)

Four jobs — `apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync` — are four separate `SyncJob`s, never merged into one `package_sync`, over one shared core extracted while building. The core holds what all four use: the item taxonomy, the plan/review/apply order, the decision flow, the batched TUI review, the machine-local file I/O and the read-failure guard (ADR-022). Each manager's own item shapes and diff stay in that manager's module — one manager's diff on the shared base would make the other three inherit inputs they never supply. All four run before `folder_sync` so software is provisioned before its data lands (decisive for flatpak, where `~/.local/share/flatpak` must exist before `~/.var/app` arrives); a snippet-installed program writes its own stock defaults as a package does. `manual_installs_sync` owns everything no package manager can reproduce and carries its own enable flag.

### Batched review inside each job (D-24)

Each package job runs plan then review then apply inside its own `execute()` and converges only what the review approved. Batching — one screen per manager per action — is a strong preference, applied where the logic permits and abandoned where it does not: a job never turns a batch into a question per item, and never complicates or omits its logic to avoid another round. A job may ask again, including after it has begun writing, when the answer it needs rests on facts this run's own changes invalidated or that no read could establish before the first write; correctness outranks batching, always. `apt_sync` asks in rounds, and only `apt_sync`. Three of its questions are scoped to the work this run APPROVES rather than proposes — a repository not raised for deletion while an approved-surviving package still uses it, a repository conflict raised only for a file an approved package makes travel, and a package marked as the target's own — none decidable while the plan is built and all decidable once the first round's answers exist: a second round, same sitting, nothing written yet. The one thing unknowable before writing is the collateral of an install whose repository this run itself writes (D-40): a third round, asked once, before the first of those installs. The other three jobs have one round. No review spans two managers (D-15), so there is no shared review phase and no coordinator.

### Diff taxonomy (D-25)

Conflicts, mismatches and unavailability are diff classes inside the job's own review: missing-on-target, extra-on-target, version-mismatch (both versions shown), origin-mismatch, origin-unavailable, unreproducible. `ORIGIN_MISMATCH` covers a package or ref installed on both machines from different vendors. `REPO_UNAVAILABLE` means the source's origin cannot be provided on the target — a statement about provenance, not about whether apt printed a candidate. There is no per-package echo of a pin or a hold: D-35 checks a pin against the target's real state, and echoing it onto every package it names would make a pinned target-only package impossible to remove.

### Transactional repository convergence (D-27 boundary)

The `/etc/apt` group is the one place D-27's continue-and-report model does not apply: it is transactional, and a group whose metadata refresh fails leaves `/etc/apt` as it found it. Continuing past a bad write would leave the target's package manager unusable, and automatic snapshot rollback does not arrive until Phase 7.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to AI agents when working with code in this repository.


## Project Overview

**PC-switcher** is a synchronization system for seamless switching between Linux desktop machines (laptops, workstations). The goal is near-complete system-state replication rather than simple user data sync.

**Project Stage**: Core infrastructure complete. Core sync functionality in development.

**Target Environment**: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, btrfs filesystem, machines connected via SSH (LAN, VPN, etc.).

## Critical Context Files

**ALWAYS READ FIRST**:
- `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` - General agent instructions for all projects
- `docs/planning/high-level-requirements.md` - Complete project vision, scope, workflow, and constraints
- `docs/adr/_index.md` - Summary of all architectural decisions

**For development work**: See `docs/dev/` for AI agent instructions:
- `docs/dev/development-guide.md` - Development expectations and workflow
- `docs/dev/testing-guide.md` - How to write tests

**Premature Analysis Warning**: Files in `docs/premature-analysis/` are early exploration work that may conflict with the High level requirements. These are **inspiration only** and MUST NOT be read automatically or treated as requirements. Only reference them when explicitly requested for specific feature planning.

**When creating or updating an ADR**: Read ADR-001 first for instructions.

## CLI Commands

```bash
pc-switcher sync <hostname>     # Sync to the named machine
pc-switcher init                # Create default config
pc-switcher logs                # Show logs directory
pc-switcher cleanup-snapshots   # Clean up old btrfs snapshots
```

## Development Commands

```bash
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format .
uv run codespell
uv run basedpyright
uv run pytest                                 # Unit tests
tests/run-integration-tests.sh                # Integration tests
tests/run-integration-tests.sh tests/integration/jobs/test_install_on_target_job.py::TestInstallOnTargetIntegration::test_install_on_target_fresh_machine   # Specific integration test
```

## Executor calls: `mutates=` unless purely read-only

Everything reaching source/target goes through `Executor` (`executor.py`), which drives `--confirm-each-command` and the verbatim DEBUG trace. `run_command`/`start_process`/`send_file`/`get_file` MUST pass `mutates="<phrase>"` unless the call is PURELY read-only — it may be omitted only when the call can change no state at all: no file content, no process state, no lock or advisory state, no package-manager database. "Changes no file content" is NOT sufficient grounds to leave a call ungated. Running a read under `sudo` does NOT make it a write: `sudo <read-only command>` is read-only. In-process changes (no shell command): `executor.declare_modification(...)`. Omitting it ships a change the user is never shown; `tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py` enforces this.

## REMEMBER
- When creating a PR on GitHub, ALWAYS set it as draft so that the integration tests don't run prematurely.
